Enum types are just ints under the hood --- enums just give
you a way of making sure the ints are disjoint, but then
that might not even be built into the wild west that is C/C++.

> 2. I'm a big fan of having an abstract base class define the interface for template patterns. Would you mind if I did this for the recorder stuff? I could then refactor everything to isolate the use of std::cout to a single line in command.hpp.

An alternative that doesn't involve virtual functions calls is
the curiously recursive template pattern (CRTP). This is what
Eigen uses rather than standard abstract base classes. But efficiency
is probably not an issue here.

The disadvantage of virtual base classes and the CRTP is that everything
needs to derive from a single class. An alternative is to template instead,
as in Boost PRNGs. There's a so-called "concept" underlying all the
PRNGs, rather than a shared abstract base class.

- Bob

It depends what you want to do with it, particularly how flexible
and performant you want it. I think the OO approach is falling out
of favor in C++ libs if Boost and Eigen are any indication.

Check out how Boost documents concepts, which needs to be done
outside of the language, and thus isn't nearly as clean at informing

to be done by reference or pointer (I'd VERY STRONGLY prefer references everywhere,
as they're always guaranteed to be defined, unlike pointers).

It could, but it's hugely inefficient to convert numbers to strings
and back to numbers again. Not much choice when reading from files
other than using a binary representation (which Marcus was advocating
given how slow inits are due to having to convert strings to numbers).
No reason we can't support that, too, among other ways to construct

Terminologically, factories are alternatives to constructors.
They have some advantages because constructors are limited in
terms of how they can be used, what functions they can call in which
orders, and so on.

The more general factory pattern has a factory object, which can
be plugged and played. So you'd pass a factory to another function
and that function would use the factory to create objects rather
than calling a constructor. Then you can easily configure which
kinds of objects get constructed in a way that's encapsulated from
the perspective of functions using it.

Nope, I didn't look at the code, and didn't understand your
language describing it because you're not using "factory" in
the usual way.

Now I'm looking at the class definition:

class var_context_factory {
public:
var_context_factory(): context_(0) {} // C++11 Upgrade to nullptr
~var_context_factory() { if(context_) delete context_; }

virtual bool create_var_context(std::string source) = 0;
stan::io::var_context* var_context() { return context_; }

protected:
stan::io::var_context* context_;
};

// This should be defined in cmdstan
class dump_factory: public var_context_factory {
public:

bool create_var_context(std::string source) {
if (context_) delete context_;

std::fstream source_stream(source.c_str(),
std::fstream::in);
if (source_stream.fail()) return false;

context_ = new stan::io::dump(source_stream);
source_stream.close();

return true;
}

};

First, this isn't a factory. A factory has a method that
returns a new instance of a particular kind of object. This
object creates something and holds a reference to it.

Second, never pass strings by value --- always by const reference.
Otherwise they get copied.

Third, holding a mutable pointer to something is a suboptimal
design decision for purposes of doc, testing, and maintenance.

I don't see what you're trying to get out of this extra layer
of indirection, so I don't see how to advise you going forward
on a better way to do it.

Here's some relevant (I hope) background.

A var_context_factory would be an abstract base class with
this signature:

class var_context_factory {
const var_context& create() = 0;
};

It has a single method to create a new var_context. It puts
the burden of freeing the created var_context on the caller,
which is probably not what you want to do.

You could also just return a var_context instead of a reference,

class var_context_factory {
var_context create() = 0;
};

but that would almost certainly require copying that the
compiler won't be able to optimize away. You can minimize
this by having the var_context destructor manage the memory
that gets allocated the same way a std::vector does.

C++11 could also mitigate most of the copying overhead by
doing a swap-based copy, which will be fine in this context.

You could also use something other than a factory object,
such as this:

class var_context_creator {
void create(var_context& c) = 0;
};

The problem with this is that the var_context needs to
be created on the outside and then passed in, and hence
can't be const. It's much much easier to reason about
classes if they are constructed in a usable state and
are immutable (const) afterward. Then you always know you
have a fully-formed instance of an object and don't need
to worry about documenting and testing getters/setters which
can mess with well-formedness of an object.

The point of any of these approaches is that you can
have multiple factory or creator instances that can be passed
by reference to other classes which wish to remain agnostic
about how things are created. I don't see the point of that
for commands.

Why not just have subclasses of var_context with their own constructors?

> I have implemented a var_context factory that handles the creation of a var_context
> from configuration data (a string) that the interfaces are responsible for implementing,
>
> var_context factory : common config (string) \rightarrow var_context instance

I was confused by this until I read the code. I think
of the colon as indicating inheritance in C++, but now I
see you're using it like f:A->B notation.

This isn't how factories work. You'd configure a particular factory
with a string then pass the factory around to whatever needed
to use it. But even if we don't call it a "factory", I don't
see the point. The whole point of using a factory is that it
hides all the implementation details from whatever is using it.

Anyway, see the comments above.

- Bob

I could not care less about what these patterns are called — Dan and I were
using factory last night and I rolled with it.

If we want to refactor these things then we need to be able to have the interfaces
define classes that handle the creation of var_contexts.  Requiring the var_context
to be created on the outside would be a giant pain because (a) the var_context
may not be necessary based on runtime info and (b) the construction of the var_context
itself may depend on runtime info.  So unless we force all the var_context implementations
to have the same constructor (and wrap any I/O internally) we have to have a
wrapper that allocates the var_context using the config information (a string indicating
the source name, possibly some addition info to select between var_context implementations) 
at runtime.

If there are other solutions then let’s consider those, but if there are not then I am
going to request more constructive comments than “this is bad for testing”, especially
when the current code is nigh untestable and requires a tremendous amount of
duplicate code in the interfaces.

       context_ = new stan::io::dump(source_stream);
       source_stream.close();

       return true;
     }

   };

First, this isn't a factory.  A factory has a method that
returns a new instance of a particular kind of object.  This
object creates something and holds a reference to it.

Second, never pass strings by value --- always by const reference.
Otherwise they get copied.

Third, holding a mutable pointer to something is a suboptimal
design decision for purposes of doc, testing, and maintenance.

I don't see what you're trying to get out of this extra layer
of indirection, so I don't see how to advise you going forward
on a better way to do it. 

Here's some relevant (I hope) background.

A var_context_factory would be an abstract base class with
this signature:

 class var_context_factory {
   const var_context& create() = 0;
 };

It has a single method to create a new var_context.  It puts
the burden of freeing the created var_context on the caller,
which is probably not what you want to do.  

You could also just return a var_context instead of a reference, 

 class var_context_factory {
   var_context create() = 0;
 };

but that would almost certainly require copying that the
compiler won't be able to optimize away.  You can minimize
this by having the var_context destructor manage the memory
that gets allocated the same way a std::vector does.

C++11 could also mitigate most of the copying overhead by
doing a swap-based copy, which will be fine in this context.

You could also use something other than a factory object,
such as this:

 class var_context_creator {
   void create(var_context& c) = 0;
 };

The problem with this is that the var_context needs to
be created on the outside and then passed in, and hence
can't be const.  It's much much easier to reason about
classes if they are constructed in a usable state and
are immutable (const) afterward.  Then you always know you
have a fully-formed instance of an object and don't need
to worry about documenting and testing getters/setters which
can mess with well-formedness of an object.

The point of any of these approaches is that you can
have multiple factory or creator instances that can be passed
by reference to other classes which wish to remain agnostic
about how things are created.  I don't see the point of that
for commands.  

Why not just have subclasses of var_context with their own constructors?

I have implemented a var_context factory that handles the creation of a var_context
from configuration data (a string) that the interfaces are responsible for implementing,

var_context factory : common config (string) \rightarrow var_context instance

I was confused by this until I read the code.  I think
of the colon as indicating inheritance in C++, but now I
see you're using it like f:A->B notation.  

This isn't how factories work.  You'd configure a particular factory
with a string then pass the factory around to whatever needed
to use it.  But even if we don't call it a "factory", I don't
see the point.  The whole point of using a factory is that it
hides all the implementation details from whatever is using it.

Anyway, see the comments above.

- Bob

and some switch statement somewhere that chooses among

given that we don't want dependencies on R or Python internals
in Stan C++.

> If there are other solutions then let’s consider those, but if there are not then I am
> going to request more constructive comments than “this is bad for testing”,

I was trying to be constructive in explaining why it
complicates class use and testing by making classes stateful rather
than immutable. Did that not make sense or do you disagree?

Until you understand why it's a problem, you won't see any
need to fix it.

If you find using variant objects too onerous (see the Boost
package), then we can pass in dummies, which won't incur much
overhead.

> especially
> when the current code is nigh untestable and requires a tremendous amount of
> duplicate code in the interfaces.

I don't see how that's relevant in designing something better.

For a constructive comment, how about making the context
object less generic and more tuned to the particular interfaces?
If there are pieces shared between optimization and sampling,
then pull those out in reusable chunks which can be validated
in chunks. The whole top-level config object doesn't need to be
shared among different samplers or between sampling and optimization.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Refactor Schmefactor
parts:
Requiring the var_context
to be created on the outside would be a giant pain because (a) the var_context
may not be necessary based on runtime info

Is an example when there's no user-specified inits, so we don't
need a var_context for the initial values?

That is one example.  If we want to have relatively self-contained functions
for all of the interfaces to call then we can’t rely on the interfaces being
able to create the var_context externally and pass it in.

I can't think of any case where it won't depend on runtime info.
Right now we use var_context instances for initialization of parameters
and for data, neither of which will be known at compile time.
But maybe you mean something different by "runtime" than the
usual definition which contrasts compile time with run time.

With the var_contexts requiring a source on construction, they are all
basically runtime allocations.

I think I see where you're going with this.  The call in
R looks like this:

 fit <- stan(..., data = list(a=val1, b=val2, ...),  ...);

If I understand your proposal, you want R to assign a name
to the list data structure, then pass the name in through
a generic nested string-based config along with the name of some
mechanism to convert the name of the data list into a var_context?

No, you are conflating two issues.

One issue is the way interfaces define a runtime configuration and
how that gets translated internally to Stan.  That is a separate
conversation.

What I am proposing here is a unified structure for input, where each
interface is able to convert a string to a var_context.  In cmdstan,
that means treating the string as a file name, creating a stream,
and using that to construct a var_context.  Rstan would have to be 
able to search the arguments by name to turn the string into an RList 
object which is necessary to construct the appropriate var_context.

The point is that any function that requires reading information in
from some external source would just require that the class handling
the construction of a var_context be specified as a template parameter.

Why not just pass in the var_context itself?  It seems just
as easy as passing in some object that constructs var_context
objects.

Because then the logic/config necessary for constructing that object
would have to be untangled a head of time, forcing us to use lots of
little functions and requiring lots of duplicated code in the interfaces.

This is the same pattern Dan has used for output and callbacks.

Or are you imagining some kind of string-only config
and some switch statement somewhere that chooses among
var_context implementations?  I don't see how that'd work
given that we don't want dependencies on R or Python internals
in Stan C++.

There’s no switch — the implementation is passed as a template parameter.
Look at the code!

For a constructive comment, how about making the context
object less generic and more tuned to the particular interfaces?
If there are pieces shared between optimization and sampling,
then pull those out in reusable chunks which can be validated
in chunks.  The whole top-level config object doesn't need to be 
shared among different samplers or between sampling and optimization.

Again, I don’t think you understand the scope of the proposed pattern.
I encourage you to look at initialize_state.hpp and how the function is
called in command.hpp to see how it would work.

>> I think I see where you're going with this. The call in

I'd say I was stepping back to look at the bigger picture
of where this is coming from and how it'll be used.

> One issue is the way interfaces define a runtime configuration and
> how that gets translated internally to Stan. That is a separate
> conversation.

Isn't that what we need to figure out whether we can do from R?
The call from R is going to look like the example above.

> What I am proposing here is a unified structure for input, where each
> interface is able to convert a string to a var_context.
Understood. I just think that's very limiting.

> In cmdstan,
> that means treating the string as a file name, creating a stream,
> and using that to construct a var_context. Rstan would have to be
> able to search the arguments by name to turn the string into an RList
> object which is necessary to construct the appropriate var_context.
Yes, that should be possible.

> The point is that any function that requires reading information in
> from some external source would just require that the class handling
> the construction of a var_context be specified as a template parameter.

Again, I understood that. I'm just not sure it's the ideal
design. Using strings to config everything is very limiting.
But as I said, I think it can work for R. Looks like you can
also do it in Python:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/932818/retrieving-a-variables-name-in-python-at-runtime

>> Why not just pass in the var_context itself? It seems just
>> as easy as passing in some object that constructs var_context
>> objects.
>
> Because then the logic/config necessary for constructing that object
> would have to be untangled a head of time, forcing us to use lots of
> little functions and requiring lots of duplicated code in the interfaces.

We're going to have to code the interfaces at some point.
They are going to need to know how to compute configs.

Are you imagining something that's purely nested strings?
Or something JSON-like?

For that, we probably are going to need to use variant
structures in order to represent values properly. That would
be preferable (to me) to using pointers and casting.
> This is the same pattern Dan has used for output and callbacks.
Where's that code?

>> Or are you imagining some kind of string-only config
>> and some switch statement somewhere that chooses among
>> var_context implementations? I don't see how that'd work
>> given that we don't want dependencies on R or Python internals
>> in Stan C++.
>
> There’s no switch — the implementation is passed as a template parameter.
> Look at the code!

I think I understand what you're trying to do.

What I don't understand is why you think having the interfaces
pass template parameters for classes, then pass arguments as strings
is easier in the sense of requiring less code duplication than having
them pass in the var_context directly. Especially if everything's
just going to be pointers cast at run-time all the way down.

Is it because you think checking the coherence of the arguments
will be easier? I don't see why that'd be the case, though, because
if you pass in a var_context, you know it's well formed by construction.
If you pass in strings, all sorts of things can go wrong at a lower
level (like passing in the wrong name) that won't be checkable until
the whole config object is created, so the whole catching and error
reporting apparatus gets much less modular because something's going to
have to stand at the top and catch everthing that can be thrown.

This seems to me that it'll break the modularity of error handling.
Sorry to keep harping on error checking and testing, but I wouldn't
be doing it if I didn't think it's very important. Same way you
want to yell at people for writing bad models, I want to yell at
people for deploying suboptimal design patterns.

I very well may not be understanding all the subtleties here,
but if so, I don't know which piece I don't understand.

>> For a constructive comment, how about making the context
>> object less generic and more tuned to the particular interfaces?
>> If there are pieces shared between optimization and sampling,
>> then pull those out in reusable chunks which can be validated
>> in chunks. The whole top-level config object doesn't need to be
>> shared among different samplers or between sampling and optimization.
>
> Again, I don’t think you understand the scope of the proposed pattern.
> I encourage you to look at initialize_state.hpp and how the function is
> called in command.hpp to see how it would work.

I think I do. I'm just leery of implementing reflection in object
code through strings and template parameters and breaking all the
modularity of config and testing so it's all done in one big object.

- Bob
